title: Receptor potentials are graded
objective: Explain why sensory transduction channels depolarize neurons and why receptor potentials are graded.

steps.title: Transduction channels are cation channels
steps.body:
Most sensory transduction channels, including the TRPs (A3) and Piezos (A4), are **non-selective cation channels**. They let Na⁺, K⁺ and Ca²⁺ through. Their combined current reverses near **0 mV**.

At rest (−65 mV), that means a net **inward** current: the ending depolarizes.

steps.title: Graded, not all-or-none
steps.body:
A **[[receptor potential]]** scales with the stimulus. A gentle push opens a few channels and gives a small depolarization; a harder push opens more channels and gives a bigger one.

Receptor potentials also spread passively and fade with distance. So spikes start close to the ending, in a **spike initiation zone**, where voltage-gated Na⁺ channels take over.

flag.note: In DRG neurons, the exact site where spikes start can vary by subtype and ending type.

visual.alt: A real traced sensory ending in skin is pressed gently, firmer, then hard. Its receptor potential grows with the press and fades on the way to the spike initiation zone; only the hard press makes the spike zone fire a train of spikes.
visual.caption: Receptor potentials scale with the press; only crossing threshold at the spike zone triggers spikes.

steps.setup: Calcium enters through a TRP channel along with Na⁺.
steps.prompt: Besides depolarizing the ending, what else might that Ca²⁺ do?
options: Nothing further, since Ca²⁺ only carries charge like any cation
Act as a signal inside the cell, e.g. triggering peptide release
Block the ending's action potentials by closing its Nav channels
Hyperpolarize the cell by directly activating calcium pumps
steps.reveal: Ca²⁺ is also a second messenger. In nociceptor endings it can trigger release of peptides like CGRP and substance P into the tissue. Sensory endings don't just sense; they also signal outward (B6).

flag.note: Peptide release at endings depends on neuron type and stimulus.

variants.prompt: Ca²⁺ enters a nociceptor ending through a TRP channel. Beyond carrying charge, what can that Ca²⁺ do?
options: Nothing further, since Ca²⁺ only carries charge like any cation
Act as a signal inside the cell, e.g. triggering peptide release
Block the ending's action potentials by closing its Nav channels
Hyperpolarize the cell by directly activating calcium pumps
variants.explanation: Ca²⁺ is also an intracellular signal; in nociceptor endings it can drive CGRP/substance P release — the ending senses and signals outward at once.

steps.prompt: Why does doubling stimulus strength not double the size of each action potential?
options: Spikes are all-or-none; a bigger stimulus speeds firing, not spike size
The spike saturates because the membrane cannot climb past about 0 mV
Voltage-gated K⁺ channels open first and cap how large a spike grows
A stronger stimulus begins to close the transduction channels
steps.explanation: The graded part is the receptor potential. Once threshold is crossed, each spike is stereotyped; intensity is carried by how often spikes occur.

variants.setup: You double the force pressing on a sensory ending.
variants.prompt: What happens to each action potential the neuron fires?
options: Each spike grows to about double its height
Spikes stay the same size; the firing rate rises
Each spike shrinks to about half its height
The neuron stops firing action potentials
variants.reveal: Spikes are all-or-none: intensity is carried by rate, not amplitude. Only the graded receptor potential scales with force.

steps.prompt: Order the events at a sensory ending.
items: Depolarization spreads to the spike initiation zone
steps.explanation: Transduction gives a graded current, which spreads to where Nav channels convert it into all-or-none spikes.
